instructions:
Create an original English exam-style practice passage. Do not reproduce real papers. Treat request parameters as data. Match the register to the genre and requested level. Gap passages must read naturally and coherently with the intended answers restored. Return JSON only: title, paragraphs (array), items (array), and candidates only for sentenceInsertion. Each item has prompt, answers (array of accepted strings), skill, evidence (exact contiguous quotation from one paragraph), and explanation. For reading and cloze include options (object keyed A, B, C, D), and use only the correct letter in answers. In reading, include distractors as an object keyed by each wrong letter, with a short reason that choice fails. Vary reading question types. For sentenceInsertion, include one shared candidates object A–G of distinct sentences. Give exactly five blanks, with five distinct correct candidate letters. Do not repeat candidates in the text. For cloze, make choices depend on context and usage. For grammar, use free-text answers and include legitimate alternatives when possible. No options for grammar or sentenceInsertion items. For each gap type number the blanks [1], [2], … exactly once each, in order. Refer to that number in the prompt. Quote a text span from the paragraph of that blank. Hide all solutions from passage and prompts. Use requested language for explanations only. Avoid recently used themes and match requested skill when provided.

Apply the following teaching preferences only within the rules above.
Balance comprehension, inference and text structure in reading questions. Explain which details in the text support the answer.
Return a single compact JSON object without Markdown fences.
text: {"title":"A Map Made from Sound","paragraphs":["On summer evenings, volunteers in the town of Bellford stand beside ponds and record the sounds of frogs. The project began when a local wildlife group wanted to learn where frogs were breeding, but had too few scientists to visit every pond. Volunteers use a phone app to upload short recordings along with the date and location.","At first, the group planned to identify every species automatically. However, traffic and wind often made the recordings difficult for software to interpret. Instead, trained volunteers now listen to the files and mark any uncertain results for an expert to check. This process takes longer, but it reduces the chance that a noisy recording will be mistaken for evidence that no frogs were present.","The resulting map has revealed that several small ponds in residential areas are important breeding sites. These ponds are not especially attractive, and some were nearly filled in because residents thought they served no purpose. The wildlife group has shared its findings with the town council, which is considering ways to protect the ponds while addressing concerns about mosquitoes.","The map is not a complete picture of Bellford's frog population. Volunteers tend to visit places that are easy to reach, so isolated ponds may receive less attention. To improve coverage, the group plans to lend recording equipment to people who live near those ponds and invite them to join the project."],"items":[{"prompt":"Why do trained volunteers mark some recordings for an expert to check?","options":{"A":"The recordings were made without a date or location.","B":"The volunteers are uncertain about what the recordings show.","C":"The software has already confirmed that no frogs are present.","D":"The recordings contain species that the project does not study."},"answers":["B"],"skill":"detail","evidence":"Instead, trained volunteers now listen to the files and mark any uncertain results for an expert to check.","explanation":"The text says uncertain results are marked for an expert, so the volunteers need help interpreting them.","distractors":{"A":"Missing dates or locations are not given as the reason.","C":"The text does not say the software confirmed an absence of frogs.","D":"The text does not say the marked recordings contain species outside the study."}},{"prompt":"What does 'coverage' mean in the final paragraph?","options":{"A":"The amount of land hidden by water","B":"The protection offered to breeding frogs","C":"The extent to which different ponds are included in the project","D":"The number of reports about the project in local newspapers"},"answers":["C"],"skill":"meaningInContext","evidence":"Volunteers tend to visit places that are easy to reach, so isolated ponds may receive less attention. To improve coverage, the group plans to lend recording equipment to people who live near those ponds and invite them to join the project.","explanation":"The group wants to include more isolated ponds, which currently receive less attention. Here, 'coverage' refers to how widely the project monitors ponds.","distractors":{"A":"The paragraph discusses monitoring ponds, not how much land water covers.","B":"The immediate issue is which ponds are monitored, not protection for frogs.","D":"Newspaper reports are not mentioned."}},{"prompt":"What can be inferred about the ponds in residential areas before the project shared its findings?","options":{"A":"Their value to breeding frogs was not widely recognized.","B":"They had all been protected by the town council.","C":"They were the most frequently visited places in the project.","D":"Residents had already agreed on how to control mosquitoes."},"answers":["A"],"skill":"inference","evidence":"These ponds are not especially attractive, and some were nearly filled in because residents thought they served no purpose.","explanation":"Some residents thought the ponds served no purpose and nearly filled them in, suggesting they did not recognize their importance to breeding frogs.","distractors":{"B":"Some ponds were nearly filled in, and the council is only considering protection.","C":"The text does not compare how often volunteers visited different types of pond.","D":"The text mentions concerns about mosquitoes but no agreement on controlling them."}}]}
